utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Igor Pantelic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Our 15-minute delay in taking the Bench this morning, was that we were canvassing a number of housekeeping matters which we should probably raise before the witness is called for re-examination. The first is that the -- there are two urgent motions which we have from the Prosecution, and we -- we would wish to know whether the Defence is in a position to indicate now, if not now, later today, whether they intend to respond. Because if they do so intend to respond, we would request a response by the end of this week and as much as both motions concern witnesses who are due to testify next week. The other matter is that I assume that counsel have considered what we raised overnight -- well, have considered overnight what we raised yesterday about whether time -- well, not time because we have the time that's why we raised it, whether they're prepared to deal with this motion that was scheduled for Friday dealing with exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is my understanding that we are filing two motions today as -- as instructed by the -- by the Trial Chamber, which refers to the motions -- the responses, I'm sorry, the responses to the -- to the OTP motion as instructed by the Trial Chamber last week. We're filing them today. If Your Honours are referring to the motions we received yesterday, we do intend to respond to that and we would do that in the -- in the time which -- which the Trial Chamber allocates for -- for our response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And concerning the -- the arguments, I am afraid, Your Honours, the Defence is not ready to argue it today, because the research is not -- is not completed until this moment, because we anticipated it is going to be Friday, and I'm afraid there has been some other matters - the coming witnesses - that we were -- we were pressed to deal with. So I'm afraid I couldn't [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's helpful to know, Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- I'm going to deal with a number of matters -- I'm sorry, I'm hidden at the moment. I am going to deal with a number of matters once the witness is finished. But an urgent decision is needed, please, on our motion of the 3rd of August, to which the Defence have already responded, I believe, to add the video relating to the killings at Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We haven't forgotten that one. We hope to have that out soonest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hope it is more than soonest because as I'm explaining, if we have to move witnesses up, which we may have to in the light of what has been happening, then the witness who is scheduled to start next Monday, we may be starting on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is that Witness 023?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And he is scheduled for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment, he is scheduled for Monday. We have a witness scheduled for Friday, plus exhumations argument, who you issued a witness summons for, and we understand from VWS that there may be problems because of visas in getting him here. So -- and apparently the witness summons has not been served, we're told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, our decision will be rendered tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, what are you basically -- Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What you are basically telling us is that we won't have a witness for Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the -- the scheduled witness, no. The witness who is due to start on Monday, should be arriving today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then you move him to the Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if we have to we will move him up. We're still hoping we will get the scheduled witness for Friday. But, as I say, as my understanding is, he will be here today and, therefore, all things being equal as he is 92 ter, if he has listened to everything, then we would be able to start him on Friday instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you have something or a witness to fill the gap on Monday then?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to move -- we're going to move people up. We hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And for Thursday, what will happen on Thursday? This Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witness who is going to start tomorrow - I'm going to explain - we cannot call another witness today and I'm going to explain why when Mr. Hannis has finished his re-examination. Because we are troubled by the matters that Your Honours raised yesterday which is this question of cross-examination estimates. Which, I may say, when we checked I have raised at least three or four times and Mr. Hannis has raised a couple of times. But I thought we could wait until after the witness is finished, because we can't call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just to have an indication as -- as I can see it now, we -- we won't have a witness for Thursday. Because the witness for Wednesday will -- the -- the Wednesday hearing will be sufficient for that witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You have given Mr. Olmsted half an hour and the estimate for cross-examination, at present, for this witness is four hours, I think, in total. So that would take us into Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I say, I appreciate that -- I don't think that the Defence were not expecting the exhumations to be brought up so quickly; in other words, today rather than Friday, and as it's their argument obviously they need a chance to prepare. But, I mean, if necessary, if we really run short on Thursday, perhaps we could do it then, the Defence having had enough notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we have Mr. Davidovic in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, good morning to you, sir. Before Mr. Hannis begins his re-examination, I remind you, you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic. Yesterday, Mr. Cvijetic, at page 13555, 13555, was asking you about the killings of the Sarajlic, Sejmanovic and Malagic families in Bijeljina in September 1992, and he asked if you were able to associate Mr. Stanisic in any way with those killings, and I don't know if it was a matter of interpretation but your answer is a bit confusing. You are recorded in the transcript as having answered that: "I was not able to associate Mr. Stanisic with that killing in any way because as far as this killing is concerned and the other killings in Bijeljina are concerned, that took place before Mico Stanisic became head of that ministry." Now, we have evidence in this case and I don't think it is contested that Mico Stanisic became the minister of the RS Ministry of Interior March 31st, 1992 or thereabout, and was the only minister of the RS MUP interior in 1992. So -- and it's clear that these killings that we're talking about are around September 24th or 25th 1992 regarding those particular three families. So can you help clarify that a little bit? Were you talking about some killings that had happened earlier in early 1992 or 1991? Because that would have been the period of time before Mr. Stanisic became the minister.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about the killings in Bijeljina, before Mico Stanisic came to head the ministry, I was referring to the period when the SDS came into power. At that time, Jesuric Predrag was chief of the public security station and serious killings happened in Bijeljina. People were being taken away. They simply disappeared and so on. This happened throughout 1991, that is to say, the second half of 1991. Then 1992, the beginning of the war in particular, when Arkan came there. And finally, the killing in September, when the family was killed. I can't remember the last name, I'm sorry. I think that when I spoke about this cycle of events I talked about all of it so I could not bring Mico Stanisic into the picture because I talked about the beginning of the war and when all these killings took place in an organised, planned fashion with a view to intimidating the Muslim population and expelling them from the area or making them flee from the area of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, I understand. Now I'm talking about particularly about those killings, September 24th, 25th, 1992, of the Sejmanovic, Sarajlic, and Malagic families. You agree Mr. Mico Stanisic was the minister of the interior of the RS at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stanisic was minister in that period of time and, again, I point out that the unit commanded by Dusko Malovic at the time -- well, at the time people were saying that that group, that unit had committed the mentioned killings, especially of the Sarajlic family. They were taken out of their house and taken to the banks of the Drina River and liquidated there. He was then minister of the interior and it is well known that he was the immediate superior of Dusko Malovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these killings were a matter of some public discussion at the time, right? There had been a press release issued by Mirko Blagojevic or the Serbian Radical Party a few days after the killings, indicating that the killings had been done by Dusko Malovic and his unit. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From citizens and other persons who were in touch with me and even from my family, from my wife, I heard that that family was brought and killed. I was in Montenegro at the time. Later on, it was a generally known thing, especially in the media that that had happened and that it was allegedly committed by Dusko Malovic's group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me it certainly would have come to Mico Stanisic's attention given the fact that it was well-known in the media in Bijeljina where the MUP headquarters were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Doesn't that call for a conclusion, Mr. Hannis? Mr. Cvijetic what is your objection? I anticipate that that is what your objection is going to be. Yes, Mr. Hannis, isn't that the problem with that question? Calls for a conclusion on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour it is does, but I don't think that -- that should prevent him from answering it. That goes to how much weight you would give that evidence. But, for example, in a drunk driving case, I -- my -- I could ask my wife if, in her opinion, that person appeared to be drunk because that is something within the realm of the average person's experience and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect, that analogy breaks down because in that case you are dealing with an observation. There is nothing wrong with the witnesses giving observation, that is what witnesses ordinarily are expected to do. But here your answer clearly calls for a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But my question is to an experienced professional policeman who lived in Bijeljina, who worked in the MUP and would know the kinds of matters that regularly come to the attention of the police. And discussion in the public where there is a press release about the killings that three local families certainly seem to be the kind of thing that a policeman in that town would know about from reading the paper, talking to people, listening to the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have the evidence of the publicity of this. We have the evidence of the fact that the number one accused was a minister at the time, and it is probably an inference, a reasonable inference, that you would, at the appropriate time, invite the Chamber to draw. But I think that's as far as you can take it as a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour. I will save that for submissions later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that event, we showed you yesterday a statement from Mico Stanisic that was submitted to the Prosecutor's office, and you saw that bundle of documents during proofing that came from the regional Prosecutor named Lija Sukalic. Do you know him? Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is Alija not Lija. I know that prosecutor personally. And I know that he was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed it yesterday and I did not deal with any one of these documents. Even the Prosecutor did not raise the issue or deal with these documents in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes I did. I showed the witness Exhibit P1543, which is the package of documents. But, Your Honours, the only reason I ask the question was that when I showed the exhibit to the witness yesterday in e-court it was listed as Exhibit P1543. I took it that that document was already in evidence. I'm informed now that apparently it has only been marked for identification. Since this witness has now testified about some portion of that, he knows the Prosecutor, the document itself appears to be in regular in form, and on page 1, the letter -- the cover letter from the prosecutor indicates this material is being sent to The Hague for its consideration. I think there is no issue that it is authenticity, and I would now ask that it be admitted into evidence rather than marked MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What is -- is there a response from the Defence? It seems to me, Mr. Cvijetic, that if only for the sake of tidiness and completeness, the MFI status should be lifted at this stage. Let's go ahead. But do you have -- do you have a response to the application?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. But not through this witness. If I'm not mistaken, these documents are dated 2004. The question was where the witness was at the time, whether he knew about the substance of all of these documents and whether he participated in any way in all of this. That was done only in 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you even have a set of 200 pages of different documents and now to admit under a single number this kind of compilation -- well, I can't even count them now. It is not one document. It is an entire investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's precisely the point and precisely why it is put together as one exhibit. It only makes sense when it is a complete package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We -- the MFI would be lifted and the document now be marked as a full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, at page 13562 yesterday, Mr. Cvijetic was asking you about provision in the -- in the law of the Republika Srpska that talked about allowing police officials from another republic to take actions within the RS. And in answer to a specific question related to that, you said that when you came to the Republika Srpska you did not come in accordance with that article but you became [sic] on a request issued by the organs of the Republika Srpska and you mention how Mr. Karadzic in his conversation with Prime Minister Panic had requested help. But I take it in that answer you're talking about your second trip to the RS with your -- with men from your unit when you came in probably early July 1992. But it was a different situation on your first visit with your men from the RS MUP when you came in probably early April. Because on that first trip, that's when Kertes and Gracanin told you needed to take vacation and volunteer to go. On that first trip when you came, you didn't wear your federal SUP insignia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained that yesterday. The first trip and the second trip, I said unequivocally how I went the first and second time, and I also talked about the authority or the Federal Secretariat in relation to the Republican Secretariat, what subordination was and when we could act in concert. I think I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic relates to Exhibit P591, which was shown to you. It's transcript page 13564. This exhibit is a report by General Tolimir about various paramilitary groups that were active on the territory in Bosnia or the RS, and it's quite a specific question I want to deal with. He said: "You will agree with me that the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, in order to deal with numerous paramilitary formations, needed support of all structures and communities of Republika Srpska; am I right?" Your answer was: "Yes." In addition to the support of those structures, would you agree it was also necessary to have the political will to do something about those paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, agree. Without that political will, I mean, that is a decisive factor in all of it, there can be no success and there can be no result. I think that that showed what the reason was, why everything was annulled after the actions we carried out in 1992 and everything went on just the way it had been. I think that there was no political will to have these problems resolved. If you remember when I talked about the meeting between General Mladic and President Karadzic in Lukavica, I said that Karadzic pointed out a particular question at the time, that it should not be allowed that a Serb should shoot at a Serb because that would cause terrible problems. And I think that throughout the war, even when illegal things did occur, when crimes were committed, when murders were committed, when persons were arrested, from the top political echelons there was always an interpretation to the effect: Let these people go, don't let a Serb arrest a Serb. And that was the opinion that prevailed, at least where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned page 13562 yesterday that you -- during the course of planning for the operation in Zvornik that was carried out in late July, that you found out that in Celopek there were Muslims detained there and that some had been killed. Did you have an opportunity to go to Celopek during that planning for the Zvornik operation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before I carried out the operation in Zvornik, I went to -- two operational reconnaissance missions. Apart from the information that I received from the structures that requested me to come there, the structures in Zvornik, I went there on my own to see where those positions were, with how many people, how strong they were, what kind of environments they had, and how I could fight them with what forces. And when I went to Celopek for the second time or passed it by, I saw members of the reserve police there at the centre securing it. And later on, I learned that inside that centre there were people who had been apprehended and taken there by force and that there had even been murders which was indeed the reason for me to make the acquaintance of the chief of the security of the VRS, Mr. Tolimir, who insisted that the army be involved, and that later on measures be taken and criminal reports filed against the perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you next a document, 1D75. Mr. Cvijetic showed this to you yesterday. And at page 13567, he -- he asked you if it faithfully reflected how the action developed. And you said: "Yes, very briefly it does reflect the situation." I had a question though, if I can see the English, I'll -- the last paragraph says: "Serb Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Interior, police detachment, together with the Serb armed forces military police members, performed this action of disarmament." There is no mention of you and your group, but you took a major part in that action, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I must say something that you won't like. When the Yellow Wasps operations in Zvornik was carried out, many of those who were in powers, and especially after the events after the end and what is going on there The Hague, all those who were involved with the Yellow Wasps and others who were involved in the events in Bijeljina, all that reflected the will of the political structures and the MUP, too, that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. The interpreter doesn't understand, can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I raised my hand to stop you because I heard in my headphones the interpreter saying, Could the witness please repeat his answer because they don't understand and can't follow you. Could you try it again. And go as slow as you possibly can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could both microphones be turned off, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about the involvement and my work in the Yellow Wasps operations, I said that in that operation that we carried out then, objectively speaking the MUP of the RS, based on the authority it received from the political structures at the time and which means from Mr. Mico Stanisic I went to Zvornik at the time and carried out the operation of the arrest of those persons. In that operation, which was rather demanding and difficult, military units also took part. The military -- it was the military judiciary at the time that processed perpetrators of war crimes and they wanted to work on those cases directly and I enabled them to do so. I asked the chief of security, Mr. Tolimir, to assign army members to do that, and Mr. Salapura was involved in the planning of the carrying out of that operation. He also a high-ranking official in the VRS and that is how they were also involved in that operation, but they were under my immediate command, they were subordinate to me, and they carried out what I had requested them to do. Later on, many of them presented that as their personal success towards some politicians, but I can say what the operation was in a -- really like and who was involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that's -- that's part of why I'm asking the question. You've told us in your statement and in prior testimony that you were basically the initiator of that operation, that you planned it, you were in overall command. But you and your unit are not mentioned in this document, and I think you told us it was signed by Goran Macar. It seems to be some sort of document maybe intended as a press release, and you're not getting any credit. Can you tell us why that is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't expect recognition or acknowledgment from anybody, especially not from Macar or the people who worked him. I worked based on the authority that I received primarily from my minister, and the reason why I came to the RS, namely the disarmament of paramilitary units, I was in authority received from Mico Stanisic and Cedo Kljajic, and I must repeat, when I received that authority nobody limited me in the planning, the detailed analysis and the carrying out of that operation. Nobody restricted me in saying you should do it this way or that way. I didn't even say to Minister Stanisic on which day I would enter Zvornik and when the operation would be conducted, nor did he ask me. But I did it totally autonomously, without anybody interfering, and I think we were able to carry it out with using the advantage of surprise. But now some individuals are trying to present it as the success of military security, and so on, but that's how they want to present it. I'm saying what it was really like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis, page 16, line 19, I believe the witness said that Mico Stanisic and Cedo Kljajic gave him the task or support for this action and it wasn't recorded. Maybe you can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, the transcript says -- there's apparently a question about something maybe missed. It says: "... Cedo Kljajic, and I must repeat when I received that authority nobody limited me in the planning." Did you say that neither Mico Stanisic nor Cedo Kljajic limited you in planning the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the ones who said that I had full authority and that they would not restrict me in any way, nor would they give me instructions as to do this or don't do that. They said, Do what you think is best to prevent that conduct and enable the illegal [as interpreted] authorities to carry out -- to perform their functions that they should.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in -- in that same conversation with them, is that when they told you that Karadzic and Krajisnik were tired of what was going on with the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I was told then that they had many comments and that even Karadzic and Krajisnik insisted that that very paramilitary formation be disarmed. Because there was much information that they were harassing people there, stealing vehicles, looting and committing all sorts of crimes. Many high-ranking politicians and people from the economy at Pale had many problems with them, and even --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was robbed of his vehicle. They made some people, including Velibor Ostojic, to eat grass when they -- when they met them, and so on. I don't know whether that is true though. But that was -- that was the talk at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters indicated they didn't get the name that you mentioned in connection with a person whose car was taken. Was that Mr. Ostojic, the minister of information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, Velibor Ostojic was mentioned as minister, but there were other persons apart from Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, a part of witness's answer was not recorded. I don't know if we want to return back or ask for verification. The part where he says that he doesn't remember if -- if Cedo Kljajic or Mico Stanisic or somebody else told him about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that correct? Is that what you said, Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said that they had informed me accordingly, but only the section about eating grass is uncertain. I'm not sure whether I heard it from them or whether I heard that later. They were talking to me about serious problems about beating people up, robbing their property, and harassing them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go next to another topic and show you Exhibit P1269. This is a document that was shown to you at transcript page 13585 by Defence counsel yesterday when he was asking you about the disciplinary measures taken against Dragan Andan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to, I think it's the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated 9th of September, 1992. And I'm sorry, I think we have to go to page 3. Do you remember seeing this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The last paragraph, item 1. It says Dragan Andan temporarily suspended and -- I don't think I need go on reading the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we go to the next page in B/C/S and the English page that shows item number 3 in this list. You were also shown item number 2 about Danilo Vukovic being disciplined. I want you to have a look at item number 3 in this list. This shows that Branko Stevic was appointed chief of the Bijeljina SJB in September 1992. Does that refresh your memory now about who would have been the chief of the SJB Bijeljina in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the SJB at the time was Sinisa Karan [phoen], I believe. But a bit earlier, he was transferred to the position of the chief of centre, possibly when Dragan was suspended. So I believe that somebody else succeeded him. It may have been Karan. I'm not sure about all this, but this man - what's his name - Dusko Adnan, was probably the acting chief, but whether he immediately succeeded Branko Stevic or there was somebody else in that position before him, I don't know, because I came in August, so there may have been some things in the preceding period that I don't know of. I'm not sure what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 13586, Mr. Cvijetic, at the bottom of the page and going on to the following page, it says: "You told us that almost all paramilitary formations entered Republika Srpska claiming they were volunteers, patriots to -- coming to fight on behalf of the Serbian people; am I right? " Your answer was: "Yes, you are." I'm not sure where you previously supposedly told us that almost all paramilitary formations entered. Would you agree that many of the paramilitary formations in the Republika Srpska were -- were home-grown, if I may say, were locals, not necessarily just people from outside the RS?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a leading question, that the witness has already been offered an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I belive that I should answer this question anyway. If you allow me, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll allow you, if the Judges will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The arrival of the paramilitary formations was something that coincided with the beginning of the war in the RS. To my mind, paramilitary formations principally were arriving from the Republic of Serbia. At the beginning through Arkan and his supporters and later there were volunteers from various areas, Serbia, Nis, Vojvodina and so on, and they were coming on their own initiative to various parts of the RS. And the local authorities more or less offered them accommodation and logistical report and everything the paramilitary formations that had come in from outside needed. I'm primarily referring to those who came in from outside. It's a fact that the paramilitary formations that had come in from elsewhere were later joined by some local thugs, those who had been trouble-makers even before because they soon found common interests and acted together. The passage where the number of 4- to 5.000 is mentioned is realistic, I believe. It's a realistic estimate for all of the RS. They were -- those were people who were bloodthirsty, eager to kill others, hoodlums in a word, and they had ambitions of their own. They are the dregs of humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing in General Tolimir's late July report about the various paramilitary groups operating in the RS, that there were a number of local groups, some of them related to the SDS? Among them there was mention of Mauzer, Ljubisa Savic, and the Serb Volunteer Guard in Bijeljina, reference to the SOS in Banja Luka and others.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. But mind you, at the beginning of the war, the SDS was trying to ignore the JNA because they considered them all Communists and that they cannot defend Serbianhood, that a new elite of the Serb people had risen and that they -- that there were not dealing with a new enlightened Serbian national consciousness and they wanted to build an army of their own. In Bijeljina, there was Mauzer. In Lubik [phoen], there was this radical. In Zvornik, there were also three to four groups. And they were basically units of the SDS party, and they did only what they were requested to do so by the party, not by the military authorities, not by the police authorities, but by the SDS party and the Crisis Staff of that party. And these are the paramilitary formations that had a local character and that were from those towns and villages. In every town they had a local leader, some warlord of sorts and who decided -- who had the last word about everything. He was the master of life and death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 22:9 it is recorded "now by the military," but I believe it should be "not by the military, not by the police authorities." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Davidovic? That seems to make sense. Is that what you meant to say, that "not by the military" instead of "now by the military."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two last topics. You -- you testified about being contacted by Mr. Mico Stanisic and meeting with him in late 2004 or early 2005. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was the only topic he asked you about in that meeting related to the September 1992 killings of those three Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe the topic was only mentioned in passing. It was not the main subject of discussion. I was asked whether anybody had spoken about that and I said yes, but as I hadn't been involved I didn't say anything then. But I did say that talking to Dusko Malovic, upon returning from Pljevlje, I spoke with him at the Bosanska villa and Dusko said to me that his unit had done that person to the exclusive orders of Drago Vukovic. But as you're coming back to the issue of the Sarajlic family, and what I said earlier, I must give a more comprehensive answer concerning that topic, if you allow me. I will be brief. I saw that for the first time when I came here to The Hague and I had the opportunity to scrutinise it in detail and I read it through, and I must return to what has been said earlier. When I was saying that Mico Stanisic was the head and that he directly commanded the unit, I replied that he was the one who brought the unit to Pale and later to Bijeljina and that he commanded it. That the duty of that unit was to secure facilities Minister Stanisic and carry out other tasks that had to do with the cabinet. Talking about the Sarajlic family and the connections of Mico Stanisic and Dusko Malovic, I must clearly state that -- how it was. When I read through the materials, the documents, I understood that the leading structures of the MUP wanted to, and in the beginning they were successful, wanted to cover up the murder. As far as I was able to tell from the documents, when the bodies were found in the morning and the citizens had reported that, the members of the reserve force went to the site, and, pursuant to the orders of the reserve commander, they threw the bodies back in the water and tried to cover up the traces. And later on, they reported to the station in Bijeljina that they had done the job, they had informed their commander, and then I believe it was Skoric and other forensic technicians went to the site and found some traces but they didn't -- they weren't able to interpret them. Drago Vukovic later on tried to present it the following way: That a collegium was held, chaired by Tomo Kovac, with the purpose of establishing a team to investigate the case, but nobody of those present ever corroborated that. There were some statements by Simic and others, but let me not go into that. Anyway, it was clear that the local leadership invested the greatest efforts, and when you remember that Muhic said, Why did you publish that? Karadzic wants me to arrest you. So they didn't want to make it public and I think that they consciously covered up -- were covering up the fact -- the facts and maybe Karadzic knew about it. Possibly only through the media. Anyway, everybody tried to -- tried not to inform Mico Stanisic of that. Speaking about Mico and Dusko Malovic as a unit, I mentioned that, but I didn't say that Mico Stanisic was, indeed, informed of the murder. I couldn't put that into the context of whether or not Mico Stanisic knew about the murder or was trying to cover it up. But later on, when the International Red Cross started looking for the persons, then it became public, that there had been a mass murder, and up to this day questions were asked why nobody had conducted an investigation. And I still fail to understand why they were unable to -- to follow that up to the end. It was very -- a very simple case. But even today, it is unresolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, lastly, at page 13590, Mr. Cvijetic asked you about whether or not Mico Stanisic had given you absolute authority to fight against paramilitaries. You said you didn't have any reason not to have that kind of full power, but you say: Mico Stanisic, he did not hinder you in any way. Although he didn't hinder you, did ever ask you, for example, to arrest Arkan, or Arkan's Men for the known crimes that they had perpetrated during their presence in the RS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that when I was sent to Bosnia the second time, to Republika Srpska, my only task was, and my obligation, was clearly defined. Namely, that in Republika Srpska, I should arrest all paramilitary formations without any constraint, and I was not hindered in any way, in terms of any kind of selection. That's the order I had from my minister at the time, Pavle Bulatovic was my minister. He unequivocally gave me full powers and he said that the prime minister, Mr. Panic, stood behind that order and that I had the full support of the organ that was sending me there and that I would also have the support of the organs of Republika Srpska. When I came to Bijeljina, Mico Stanisic talked to me, as did Cedo Kljajic, and they said to me then that, regardless of name, gender, everything that had happened, wherever it is my assessment that the paramilitaries took power and did unlawful things, I could arrest them and so on. The first day I came to Bijeljina, in the SUP, I found Pejo, a self-styled general who headed that service. I found Sasa, who introduced himself as the commander of the police station in Bijeljina. And on that day, that Pejo slapped a Muslim policeman in the face, one of my policemen. Simic was his name. I knew him from earlier on. He slapped him, I don't know why, I don't know for what reason. At that moment I entered the office of the chief and then he came to me. He started gesticulating and he was shouting who was I, and so on and so forth. He wore the insignia of a chief inspector of the police that I had as well, although I was an official organ, and I had received the insignia through regular procedure and I had that as an officer of that rank and he put these insignia on just like that. I said, Who sent you? And I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because the interpreter said she didn't hear -- didn't understand the rest of the sentence. You've talked about this in your prior testimony and in your written statement. Can I -- can I stop you and just ask you a couple specific questions. Sasa and Pejo that you just mentioned, were they Arkan's Men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They fled that very moment. They left the building. They fled from Bijeljina and they never returned to Bijeljina. None of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good. With regard to Arkan, you've told us in your statement and I quote, paragraph 125: "Mico Stanisic had made a deal with Arkan for him to come into Sarajevo and occupy any territory he wanted and he could take whatever he wanted and take it to Serbia." So it's true Mico Stanisic never asked you specifically to arrest Arkan because he had a deal with him to allow him to loot; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, a deal, in the sense of Mico Stanisic calling them to Sarajevo and giving them this possibility. I mean, I heard that at Ratko Mladic's when I first spoke to him at Lukavica at the garrison there. That's when Ratko told me that there was lootings going on, and so on, and that Mico had called to Sarajevo, allegedly, the members of Arkan's Guard and gave them certain rights. I think that they were talking about Bascarsija and said, Look you can take whatever you want, whatever you liberate, whatever you take in that sense, all of that is yours. That's what General Ratko Mladic said to me then when he was telling me how these paramilitaries were not coming spontaneously or by accident, but rather that they were enjoying somebody's support. However, in later procedures that I undertook in order to disarm paramilitaries, Mico Stanisic never said, Do not arrest Arkan or whoever. I actually have to say that, had I had the opportunity to arrest him, I would have done it with pleasure, and if I had any possibility to come across him, I would have arrested him with pleasure. I would have brutally tied his hands and brought him before a court of law and then I would see what would happen. There was no hindrance in that sense. It's not that Mr. Mico Stanisic said, Do not arrest Arkan or Arkan's forces, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, may have I one question to you, just for clarification. Because you told us today that the paramilitary groups which were formed locally, were groups that were controlled by the SDS and by the Crisis Staffs but not by the army. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, through other evidence which we have heard in this trial, we have been led to understand that members or even groups that were characterised as local paramilitary groups were, from time to time, resubordinated to the army. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify. From time to time, when these paramilitary formations came, I mean, they all came with the purported wish and intention to place themselves under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. The Army of Republika Srpska, the dilemma was, at first who was whose army. Would the JNA take over the function of the Serb army or would another army be established exclusively under the authority of the SDS. At first, they did place themselves under the command of the army with the intention of going to the front line but that was only at the very outset. Later on, they chose whether they would go and whose command they would place themselves under and usually they don't want to be under anybody's command. And then when they enter the kind of relationships they did, they freely did what it was that they wanted to. I mean, they barged into state agencies, I'm primarily referring to the SUP. Took driver's licence, traffic licences. They took weapons from homes and permits for these weapons, and also if they took things that belonged to people who did not come from that particular town, for instance, or if there were -- they belong to persons -- if vehicles, for instance, belonged to persons who were from the Croat Federation then they would take that away, and later on they looted only the property of Muslims. They looted their property, they expelled them, they even killed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did, in Bijeljina, any of the paramilitary groups attempt to put themselves under the command of the police; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the groups to put themselves under the command of the police? Did I understand that properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That was my question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no attempts to be placed under the command of the police. For example, when Arkan came to Bijeljina, he took over the function of the police. And he is the one who decided what the police would do. It's not that he would be placed under the command of the police. He took over the function of the police. That very same day, he appointed his own man as a chief there, a self-styled general called Pejo, then this Sasa who left the army, he was appointed head of the station and he decided what would be done. The police did not try to oppose them or did not oppose them as such. When Arkan came, and when he established that camp that they had near the Drina River, in fact, in Bijeljina, they liberated Bijeljina. I shall take the liberty of using that word. That's how they treated themselves. They treated themselves as liberators. They were taking things away from people. They started killing Muslim the very first day and looting their property. They were taking their property out of Bijeljina. I can only tell you a few details. For instance, they took a fire brigade truck that had been paid for by the citizens themselves, citizens themselves had contributed to the payments for that vehicle and they took that. They also took the buses of Transturisty from Tuzla. And, for example, they barged into a department store and they took all sort of goods that were there. Then, in the SUP, for instance, they took files, operative files of criminals. They even entered the court and they broke safes in the court, and Jesuric Predrag was the head of the police at the time, and they hid in the police station. Imagine, they had orders not to leave. The police were ordered to sit there in the SUP and during that time, the paramilitaries, headed by Arkan, did what they did and that was presented as normal state of affairs. No one wanted to say a word about that, no one wanted to oppose that, because allegedly they greeted Arkan as a liberator. Well, later on, they said that, Yes, he did liberate us but he liberated us of people and property, objects. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when exactly was this; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the beginning of April, April/May. Beginning of April. I think it was the 1st of April, that's when it started, and it was in April/May. When they liberated Bijeljina of things that they looted and people they killed, then they went to liberate, as it were, Zvornik in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And do you know if these events were reported up through the system to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, the MUP was comprehensive. At that moment the CSB was in Tuzla. The ministry was in Sarajevo. I don't think that anyone ever reported anything about that at the time. I read an interview that was given by Jesuric Predrag, I read it the other day over here, and he says unequivocally, thanks to him, I mean, he's talking about me, I made it possible for Arkan to liberate Bijeljina and I did not want to inform the centre in Tuzla or Sarajevo because why would I inform them when they are not helping me in this way. They are just asking us to withdraw weapons and to decrease the level of personnel in the police. That is what he said. He thought that they were in power now, their time had come, and they could do whatever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So just to conclude, to your knowledge, the CSB in Tuzla was never informed of the events in Bijeljina and Zvornik. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm absolutely sure that no one ever informed Tuzla about that, let alone Sarajevo. I have never found any trace of that or any information that anyone had ever done any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Davidovic, for your testimony before the Tribunal. You are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do want to tender his 92 ter package before he's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there any objections to anything that comprises the 92 ter package?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not for the time being, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there are two transcripts, if I'm not wrong, it's 1046 -- 10476 and 10477. Why -- why should they be in your package? If I'm not wrong, it's two times four pages, and witness -- it is not -- it is not a testimony of the witness. It is just procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I recall, I don't have those in front of me right now, but there was an issue concerning the cross-examination of that witness, where, in my view, in the argument of the Prosecution at the time, that was something very unethical, allegations made that he had committed crimes and stolen property from Muslims, when it came obvious that those alleged victims were contacted and said no such thing ever happened. We wanted to put that in because you're going to have evaluate this witness's credibility, and, in my view, if you didn't see how that eventually played out and was resolved, you might think there was something to the Defence allegations in that case that this witness had been engaged in some sort of illegal activity. I think the procedural matters, if those are the pages, I believe they are, and eventually resulted in a finding by the Trial Chamber that there was no good-faith basis for asking those questions and the Trial Chamber was going to give no weight to those allegations, that's why I put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I be excused then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the 92 ter package is now admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Registry will assign exhibit numbers in due course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, your housekeeping matters are they such that we should take a break and return?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's going to take me some time to resolve matters because I want to deal with the whole question of witnesses who are coming here and the Defence [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, before we take the break, I would like to know whether there's any chance that you could be ready to engage in the exhumation discussion on Thursday instead of Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it depends how early we will adjourn today because I have to prepare the next witness, and -- and I'm cross-examining the next witness. If we adjourn earlier, I will be ready to do it on Thursday. If not, then it is going to be Friday, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Because I -- I'm asking it because that could help us with avoiding the loss of an entire court day so let's see what happens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm -- believe me, I'm willing to assist the Trial Chamber as well as anybody else to -- to speed things as much as possible. But I cannot multiply myself, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday I heard Your Honours' remarks at the end of the proceedings about the, as it were, the non-sitting time because witnesses weren't available. Can I start what I'm about to say by simply reminding Your Honours that I'm sure Your Honours don't need reminding that if there is spare time, there are still some 26 or so undealt with motions, in particular, one that goes back to May of last year, which we -- I haven't had a ruling on, not to mention 13 or so where we've had part rulings, oral rulings with written decisions to follow. So, I mean, there is -- can I just put it on that basis, if there is time available, there are still those matters outstanding. However, on the issue of the gap that has been appearing recently with witnesses, largely it's because of the cross-examination estimates. Now, Your Honours, we've been raising this periodically since effectively March of last year when this started, but it has gotten a lot worse in recent months. And on the 12th of April, indeed I raised the very question about whether or not we should abide by, when planning witnesses, the cross-examination estimates that were given. In fact, it was more in the context of whether Your Honours were proposing to limit cross-examination as opposed to what's happening now, and the upshot was we were told that the Defence hadn't really exceeded the -- as it were, the allowance that was given for cross-examination, and, at the end of the discussion, Judge Harhoff said that, you, the Trial Chamber, would see how it went. Your Honour, we did a survey yesterday of the estimates that we were given and the actual time taken for cross-examination, and in some cases, it -- it's really been pretty dreadful. In most cases, cross-examination has not taken as long as the Defence told us. In some particular cases, for example, this is going back some time now, but for ST-150, the estimate of cross-examination was two hours, and neither team cross-examined. For ST-189, it was six hours in total. One team -- the Stanisic team didn't cross-examine at all, and the Zupljanin team took 1.5 hours. For ST-127, the estimate altogether was four hours and 15 minutes. The actual total time was 54 minutes, and no cross-examination from the Zupljanin team, but they were the 15 minutes, and I think that was just right. That is effectively what has been happening and because we have been abiding by the decision that Your Honours took that we should take cross-examination into account when arranging for witnesses that's why there has been, by and large, these gaps. It has not helped also, I'm afraid, by the age-old problem, which I have raised again on a number of occasions, the Defence requests to see the witnesses. For example, the reason we can't call tomorrow's witness today is both Defence asked to see him. He arrived yesterday morning. They saw him during the afternoon. VWS taken him back to the hotel at 5.00 unless there is a good reason not to. And as we have pointed out, we thought it's oppressive to have the Defence seeing them and then the Prosecution, so they become absolutely exhausted when they are going through different sorts of things. That is an added, extra, reason why we can't just go -- or we haven't been able to call witnesses, as it were, one after the other. Your Honours, our suggestion is simply this: We will, from now on, ignore the estimates that we're given by the Defence when arranging for witnesses. We will, as an express, back-fill so that we always have witnesses available. Now, effectively the only way we can do that at this stage of the case because we're coming to the end, as it were, of the witnesses who have been witnesses all along, is to back-fill with the witnesses who will be coving the adjudicated facts because they're short. In order to do that before the site visit, we need Your Honours to rescind the six-week gap that you ordered between disclosure and calling the witness. We have disclosed for I think the last launch will go out today. We will have disclosed for everything for the witnesses we propose to call viva voce. Those searches have been completed. In most cases, very little has been disclosed, one document maybe a couple. Transcripts a statements had already been disclosed beforehand. So if Your Honours want us to make sure that we always have a witness available, if cross-examination is shorter than anticipated, then we are asking Your Honours to rescind the six weeks and turn it into -- I think we can -- if it's four weeks, we can start calling witnesses from, I think, next week. So that's -- that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. We did touch upon this issue yesterday, and I think I recall that Mr. Zecevic told us that he had, in fact, notified the Prosecution that he would probably not need the -- was it six hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Six hours required for the witness yesterday. And so the practical issue seems to be that the Defence teams provide the Chamber and the Prosecution with an estimation of the time they will need for cross-examination, and they do so quite far ahead of the witnesses' actual appearance in court. And in that situation, I understand that, to be on the safe side, most Defence teams would tend to - just do be sure - tend to overestimate a bit the time they might need so that we do not come into the embarrassing situation that we have to keep witnesses here much longer than they had anticipated. So that's -- that's the starting point. But then, as we get closer to the time when the witness is actually appearing, apparently the Defence is able to then reassess its time -- the time that it needs for its cross-examination. And I was under the impression that the Defence teams, by and large, do notify the Prosecution, I don't know how much time in advance, but I would imagine about a week or ten days perhaps, prior to the witness's arrival, that they will need this amount of time or less. So my question is: What is really the practice between the parties about the communication that takes place between the two parties about the time that is needed for -- for chief and cross? Is there any communication and what is the practice?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The estimates, as Your Honours say, fairly well in advance so that we can plan when the witnesses come. We do not get told at all, sometimes, unless we ask, Are you actually going to take six hours with this witness. If we're told, we're told when the witness here or at court. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in my understanding, that is perhaps the issue that needs to be ruled upon by the Chamber, or to be looked upon by the Chamber that we should perhaps try to have agreement in the courtroom about a minimum time for the Defence to notify the Prosecution and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do not overlap, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. The difficulty, Your Honour, is this: That it has to be further in advance because of VWS organising not only passports and the rest of but visas. And this is one of the problems with the witness that we want to call on Friday, I'm told, is that it takes five days, according to VWS, to organise a visa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's hear the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will speak in Serbian in order to be very clear. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to be completely fair to our friends from the Prosecution. Immediately before the beginning of their examination-in-chief, we do state that our cross-examination of that witness will be shorter. That is because that is the first moment when we are in a position to realistically determine how much time we will need for the cross-examination of the witness. Because, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is that after you have seen the witness? Is that the moment you say you can realistically estimate the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If that witness is willing to speak to the Defence team. Allow me just to provide a complete explanation. A certain number of months in advance, we state our estimates of the duration of our cross-examination. You must understand, Your Honours, that most witnesses are viva voce witnesses. To us, that means that the number of hours intended to be consumed by the Prosecution in the examination-in-chief directly affects the estimate of our cross-examination. It happens and quite naturally to my mind that the Prosecution says, Yes, we did want -- or intended to question the witness for four hours but now we will take only two hours after all, and that certainly effects our estimate of the duration of our cross-examination. Likewise, there have been cases when the Trial Chamber imposed restrictions on the OTP regarding an examination-in-chief of a certain witness. To my mind, it is essential that the rationale determined at the very beginning of the trial with regard to the overall time of the cross-examination or the examination-in-chief respectively will not be infringed upon and it will not until the end of the trial. On Thursday, we will receive a list of witnesses for the following week. That is the moment which three or four witnesses will be here in that week. And it is only then that we can sit down and analyse over the weekend who these witnesses are and what they are expected to say, irrespective of our preparatory work with regard to those witnesses. Because in the meantime, there have been witnesses who testified about some issues that we had intended to ask the witness we had yesterday or the day before about. And then we feel that there is no need for us to repeat the same thing over and over again if some facts have already been established. That is why it is very difficult for us to give a precise estimate. It's a special situation when we speak to the witness, that is, when we are giving the opportunity to interview him or her, when the witness agrees to speak to us. During that interview, we can establish that the witness has knowledge about some facts that are relevant to this trial, and then, naturally, we try to speak to that witness and try to turn his testimony useful for the Trial Chamber, and it is in this sense that we -- or in this way that we estimate the duration of time needed for our cross-examination. I believe that this suffices as an explanation. As regards our right to interview witnesses, I believe that is not contentious. We have explained several times why it is impossible for us to examine witnesses in their place of residence because the trial is in progress. The only reasonable situation or variant is that we interview the witness here in The Hague, if the witness agrees. That is the cheapest resolution, the most reasonable solution, and the least time-consuming one. It is absolutely reasonable, therefore, to my mind for witnesses to arrive one day in advance, which we have proposed quite some time before this day. Any other variant would be much more expensive and demanding in many ways. That is why we think that the witness should arrive one day in advance, and if he states that he is willing to speak to the Defence, then he should be here a day in advance, in order not to -- not to disturb the proofing by the OTP. As regards the latest submission by Ms. Korner, as regards the six weeks, I must say that it is completely unacceptable. It is physically impossible for us to scrutinise these very comprehensive documentation unless we have six weeks from the date we received the documents. We reached a comprise with the OTP with regard to witness who were coming under Rule 92 bis and we made an offer to reduce that period to four weeks, but that is all we can do. If anything else is unacceptable to us because it is quite impossible for us to scrutinise the entire documentation in less time than six weeks. I hope that I have been able to have been of assistance to the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two things which arise from that. The first is the Defence are given a batting order, which is the slightly casual expression for the witnesses, in advance of just the week before, the actual specific witnesses. But they know which witnesses are coming up and at the moment, they know, because effectively, as I say, we're coming to the end of the original list of witnesses, so they know exactly who is coming up. The second matter is this. Your Honour, I've raised this before, and I'm simply mentioning now, as Mr. Zecevic brought it up, we've said over and over again we object to this business of the Defence seeing the witness just before they testify. Your Honours effectively made it clear that we should carry on with this. We still object to it, and I want it firmly, as it were, in the open, because of the way that the proofing is conducted, and I'm afraid that we are unhappy with it. We're unhappy that if -- unless witnesses specifically say that they want the OTP present, if they say they don't mind if the OTP is present, that the -- the Defence are objecting to the OTP being there, and this is raising problems all round. But that's an ancillary issue, but it's one of the ways, of course, that we could cut down on the wasting of time. I mean, there is no question about it. If we go back to what we originally said, which was the Defence must see these witnesses in advance. So there's that. Your Honour, it's a matter for Your Honours. As I say, the only way we can really fill in now is if we start to bring up the new witnesses to testify about the adjudicated facts. Otherwise we're left in the same position, that we -- we may well have gaps if the cross-examination estimates are wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- on the application, as I understand it to be an application, for an order that the time for the Defence -- sorry. The time between the notice and the calling of the witness be abridged from the six weeks, that's something that we will discuss and revert to the parties at the next sitting. There are two observations that I would make before we rise. One is that the proposal, as I understand it, or it may be as high an intension which Ms. Korner has stated about back-filling, to use her word, in terms of having the witnesses here, the -- that may be a solution. It is not something that I think the Chamber could or should order at this stage because the -- as would have been obvious from what would have been said in court yesterday, in addition to the -- whereas, the Chamber is bound to take into consideration the primary consideration of VWS, in terms of expense, the Chamber has an additional duty as Judges to ensure that it doesn't impose requirements that cause unnecessary distress to witnesses who are already under pressure by having to travel to The Hague to give evidence in -- in this matter, which is a heightened form of stress than that which witnesses always experience, and that is something that we will always have to bear in mind. The final observation relates to Ms. Korner's opening statement about the time not spent in court being used for other purposes. Of course, the Chamber is appreciative of the anxiety which parties would have that such motions as are outstanding are dealt with and expedited and finally disposed of as soon as possible. But, of course, the concern that we expressed about time lost in court is in the context of the -- what is well known to practitioners, although non-practitioners often miss the point, that a court, any court, is involved with work while sitting but that the bulk of its work done while it is not sitting, and the Chamber is keenly aware of the responsibility it has to deal with those motions in its non-sitting time, but it was its sitting time that the concern was expressed about, in terms of the time lost. Because that time is irrecoverable, and that is the context. So the -- we would rise now and as I said, the next -- when we resume we would attempt to respond to -- yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of other short matters that I'd like to deal with. First, can I repeat my request so that it is quite clear that if the Defence, in their objections to the exhumation evidence, wish to rely on any authority from this Tribunal or from national jurisdictions, they should let us know 24-hours in advance. We will do the same. Second matter is this, and that's really to do with the site visit which is not far away now, and can I just raise this for Your Honours to consider. We were all wondering if it would assist if we were to provide in advance of the site visit, a booklet which will have a photograph for each of Your Honours of the particular site that you're going to see and with a page for any notes that you -- you want to make. Because, if so, we can organise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. We -- we gratefully accept the Prosecution's offer to have these booklets, and from previous experiences with site visits we know that they are extremely useful. Would it be possible not only to include photographs of the crime sites that we are going to visit, but also to have the relevant excerpts from the testimonies of the witnesses that relate to these crime sites? So that we are able to consult on the spot what the witnesses actually said and then be guided also by the photographs. I know that it has been done in previous site visits where it was considered to be of great assistance, but I'm also aware of the fact that it is an extra burden on the Prosecution to identify those places and to have them included in the log-books but it would be useful if could you have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say this. That I will say yes we can do it, subject to being told firmly, no, we can't or that we will have a problem with that. But I will say yes, for the time being, Your Honours, and hope that that works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And also the relevant maps that need to go with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. If Your Honours -- Your Honours were given, I think, a booklet of -- of the Croatian ethnic-type maps which I think will cover nearly everything that -- that -- that you're going to see. We noticed that Your Honours had added Renovica to the itinerary. Can we just point out that it appeared that Your Honours thought that it was part of Pale town. It is actually not. It is something like 30 kilometres away. But just so Your Honours -- because it Renovica/Pale town. So ... And, Your Honours, I'm sorry. There was one final matter. There was one other video that we've asked for leave to add. The witness who is going to deal with that is due to testify in a fortnight's time. The motion was filed -- so if Your Honours are considering the video which we would like for the witness either on Friday or Monday, there's also the other video filed on ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, can I say we filed a motion, I'm trying to remember the date. The Defence has responded. We were going to apply for leave to respond to their response today, but just to point out a couple of matters. But, in any event, if Your Honours feel you have got enough information about that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, I think -- something on which I touched at the beginning, the two motions filed -- thank you, Ms. Korner. This is really for the Defence. The two motions filed yesterday, could we have a response by end of business Thursday? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we rise now to resume at -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question before the break, Mr. Zecevic, about the exhumation discussion, are you able in a position to tell us whether it could happen Thursday, if time permits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can I -- can I inform the Trial Chamber in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning - I'm not sure which courtroom - but we will all be alerted at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of August, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.34 a.m.,
